passages.text:
### Case Study 1: The Geometry of Parallel Tracks & Crossings
In railway design, two parallel tracks l and m are laid out across flat ground and intersected by a straight crossover line t, acting as a transversal. Civil engineers monitor the track intersection angles to ensure safety and precision. The acute angle formed between track l and transversal line t is measured to be 65°.

### Case Study 2: Historical Indian Mathematics & Rhythmic Poetry
In ancient Indian prosody, Pingala, Virahāṅka (c. 700 CE), and later Hemachandra analyzed poetic meters composed of short syllables (*laghu*, 1 beat) and long syllables (*guru*, 2 beats). The number of rhythmic patterns for n beats forms the Virahāṅka sequence: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, \dots where each term after the second is the sum of the two preceding terms.

### Case Study 3: The Ancient Cistern and Fountain Problem
In his commentary on Brahmagupta's *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta*, the 9th-century mathematician Caturveda Pṛthūdakasvāmī posed a problem of filling a public reservoir: Four distinct fountains fill a cistern. The first fountain takes 1 full day, the second takes 1/2 day, the third takes 1/4 day, and the fourth takes 1/5 day.

questions.question: Two straight lines intersect at a single point on a flat plane. If one of the angles formed is 72°, what is the measure of its vertically opposite angle?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Recall the property relating vertically opposite angles formed by intersecting lines.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 108° is the supplementary angle forming a linear pair, not the vertically opposite angle.[cite: 4]
Correct. Vertically opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines are always equal.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. This is the complementary angle (90° - 72°).[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Vertically opposite angles are equal to the given angle (72°).[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: When two straight lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles are always equal to each other[cite: 4]. Hence, the opposite angle is 72°[cite: 4].

questions.question: If two adjacent angles form a linear pair and one angle measures 115°, what is the measure of the other angle?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Linear pair angles lie on a straight line and sum to a straight angle.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Correct. Angles in a linear pair add up to 180°, so 180° - 115° = 65°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 180° - 115° = 65°, not 75°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. This is the vertically opposite angle, not the adjacent supplementary angle.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Linear pairs are bounded by 180°.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: By definition, the sum of two angles forming a linear pair is 180°[cite: 4]. Therefore, the other angle is 180° - 115° = 65°[cite: 4].

questions.question: What is the maximum number of distinct angle measures formed when a transversal intersects two parallel lines?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between corresponding, alternate, and linear pair angles.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. This only occurs if all angles are perpendicular (90°).[cite: 4]
Correct. All 8 angles consist of just two distinct values: an acute angle θ and its supplementary obtuse angle 180° - θ (or just one value if perpendicular).[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Four distinct angle measures can occur only when the two lines are non-parallel.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Due to vertical and linear pair relationships, 8 distinct angles can never occur.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: When two lines are parallel, corresponding and alternate angles are equal[cite: 4]. Thus, the 8 angles reduce to at most 2 distinct measures (an angle and its supplement)[cite: 4].

questions.question: In the context of parallel lines intersected by a transversal, what is the sum of interior angles on the same side of the transversal?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Check the relationship between co-interior angles.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Co-interior angles are supplementary, not complementary.[cite: 4]
Correct. Interior angles on the same side of the transversal add up to 180°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 360° is the sum of four right angles.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. They are only equal if both are right angles (90°).[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: Interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary and always sum to 180° when lines are parallel[cite: 4].

questions.question: A square sheet of paper is folded in half horizontally, then in half horizontally again, and once more horizontally. How many parallel horizontal crease lines are created across the unfolded sheet?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Recall the formula 2ⁿ-1 or count the internal crease lines for n folds.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 3 creases result from 2 folds.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 5 is the total number of parallel lines including the 2 sheet borders after 2 folds.[cite: 4]
Correct. 3 successive folds divide the paper into 2³ = 8 strips, creating 8 - 1 = 7 internal parallel crease lines.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 8 is the number of sections, not crease lines.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: Each horizontal fold doubles the sections: after 3 folds, there are 2³ = 8 equal sections, which means there are 8 - 1 = 7 internal parallel creases[cite: 4].

questions.question: A transversal crosses two lines l and m. A pair of alternate interior angles measure (3x + 10)° and (2x + 35)°. For what value of x are the lines l and m parallel?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Alternate interior angles must be equal for lines to be parallel.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Correct. Equating 3x + 10 = 2x + 35 gives x = 25.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Substituting 15 gives 55° ≠ 65°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Check the linear equation solving steps.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Substituting 35 gives 115° ≠ 105°.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: For lines l and m to be parallel, alternate interior angles must be equal: 3x + 10 = 2x + 35 ⇒ 3x - 2x = 35 - 10 ⇒ x = 25[cite: 4].

questions.question: Based on Case Study 1, what is the measure of the obtuse angle forming a linear pair with the 65° track angle?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Sum of angles on a straight line is 180°.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 180 - 65 = 115, not 125.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 65° is the acute vertically opposite angle.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Check arithmetic subtraction from 180°.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: The obtuse angle and the 65° acute angle form a linear pair: 180° - 65° = 115°[cite: 4].

questions.question: Based on Case Study 1, what is the measure of the alternate interior angle on the parallel track m?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Alternate interior angles between parallel lines are equal.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Alternate interior angles are equal, not complementary.[cite: 4]
Correct. Since tracks l and m are parallel, alternate interior angles are equal to 65°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 115° is the consecutive interior angle.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. The lines are not perpendicular.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: Since the tracks are parallel, the alternate interior angle to the acute 65° angle is also exactly 65°[cite: 4].

questions.question: In the figure below, lines l and m are parallel and cut by transversal t. What is the value of ∠ x?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Identify whether ∠ x and the 50° angle are alternate interior or consecutive interior angles.[cite: 4]

diagram.description: Two parallel horizontal lines cut by a transversal showing an interior angle of 50 degrees.
diagram.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.plot([-3, 3], [1, 1], color='#0F172A', lw=2)
ax.plot([-3, 3], [-1, -1], color='#0F172A', lw=2)
ax.plot([-2, 2], [2, -2], color='#2563EB', lw=2)
ax.text(2.5, 1.2, '$l$', fontsize=12, color='#0F172A', ha='center', va='bottom')
ax.text(2.5, -0.8, '$m$', fontsize=12, color='#0F172A', ha='center', va='bottom')
ax.text(1.8, -1.8, '$t$', fontsize=12, color='#2563EB', ha='center', va='bottom')
ax.text(0.3, 0.7, '$50^{\circ}$', fontsize=11, color='#DC2626', ha='left', va='center')
ax.text(-0.5, -0.7, '$x^{\circ}$', fontsize=11, color='#DC2626', ha='right', va='center')
ax.set_xlim(-3.5, 3.5)
ax.set_ylim(-2.5, 2.5)
ax.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('diagram.svg', format='svg', bbox_inches='tight')

options.explanation: Correct. The two angles are alternate interior angles between parallel lines, hence x = 50°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 130° is the consecutive interior angle on the same side.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Check alternate interior angle equality.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. The angles are in alternate positions across the transversal.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: The marked angle x and the 50° angle lie on alternate sides of the transversal between the two parallel lines, making them equal alternate interior angles: x = 50°[cite: 4].

questions.question: Two lines AB and CD are cut by transversal EF. If a pair of interior angles on the same side of the transversal measure 110° and 75°, which statement is true?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Sum the two interior angles and compare with 180°.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Parallel lines require co-interior angles to sum to exactly 180°.[cite: 4]

options.text: The lines will intersect on the side of these angles
options.explanation: Incorrect. The sum is 110° + 75° = 185° > 180°.[cite: 4]

options.text: The lines will intersect on the opposite side of these angles
options.explanation: Correct. Since 110° + 75° = 185° > 180°, the interior angles on the other side sum to 360° - 185° = 175° < 180°, where they must meet (Euclid's fifth postulate).[cite: 4]
Incorrect. The angles are neither 90° nor do the lines form right angles.[cite: 4]

questions.correctAnswer: The lines will intersect on the opposite side of these angles
questions.explanation: The sum of the interior angles on this side is 185° > 180°[cite: 4]. Therefore, the sum on the opposite side is 175° < 180°, which means the lines will converge and meet on that opposite side[cite: 4].
questions.answer: The lines will intersect on the opposite side of these angles

questions.question: If line p is parallel to line q, and line q is parallel to line r in the same plane, what is the geometric relation between line p and line r?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Consider lines parallel to the same line.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Parallelism preserves orientation.[cite: 4]

options.text: They are parallel to each other
options.explanation: Correct. Lines that are parallel to the same line in a plane are parallel to each other.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. They never intersect.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Parallelism is transitive in Euclidean plane geometry.[cite: 4]

questions.correctAnswer: They are parallel to each other
questions.explanation: In a plane, two lines that are parallel to a third line are always parallel to each other[cite: 4].
questions.answer: They are parallel to each other

questions.question: In a zigzag figure where ray LM ∥ PQ, ∠ LMN = 40°, ∠ MNO = 96°, and ∠ OPQ = 52°, what is the measure of the reflex/interior angle ∠ NOP?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Draw auxiliary parallel lines through vertices N and O parallel to LM.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. This is the measure of ∠ MNO.[cite: 4]
Correct. Through N, drawing a line parallel to LM splits 96° into 40° (alternate) and 56°. A parallel line through O gives alternate angles 56° and 52°, summing to 56° + 52° = 108°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Check the subtraction 96° - 40° = 56°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. The components are 56° and 52°.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: Drawing parallel lines through N and O: the angle of 96° at N is composed of 40° (alternate to ∠ LMN) and 96° - 40° = 56°[cite: 4]. At vertex O, ∠ NOP splits into alternate angles 56° and 52° (alternate to ∠ OPQ)[cite: 4]. Thus, ∠ NOP = 56° + 52° = 108°[cite: 4].

questions.question: In parallelogram ABCD, side AB ∥ CD and AD ∥ BC. If ∠ ADC = 60° and diagonal AC splits ∠ DAB such that ∠ DAC = 65°, find the measure of ∠ CAB.[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Consecutive interior angles ∠ ADC and ∠ DAB sum to 180°.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Correct. Since ∠ ADC + ∠ DAB = 180°, ∠ DAB = 120°. Therefore, ∠ CAB = 120° - 65° = 55°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. ∠ DAC = 65°, but the total is 120°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 60° is ∠ ADC.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 120° - 65° = 55°.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: Since AB ∥ CD with transversal AD, consecutive interior angles add to 180°: ∠ DAB = 180° - 60° = 120°[cite: 4]. Since ∠ DAB = ∠ DAC + ∠ CAB, we have ∠ CAB = 120° - 65° = 55°[cite: 4].

questions.question: In the given configuration, AB ∥ CD ∥ EF. Transversal line segment BE makes an angle ∠ BEF = 55°. If line segment EA ⊥ AB, find the interior angle x = ∠ ABE.[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Find ∠ BAE = 90° and use alternate angles between AB and EF.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Correct. Since AB ∥ EF, consecutive interior angles ∠ BAE + ∠ AEF = 180° ⇒ 90° + ∠ AEF = 180° ⇒ ∠ AEF = 90°. Thus ∠ AEB = 90° - 55° = 35°. In right \triangle ABE, ∠ ABE = 180° - (90° + 35°) = 55°, so its obtuse angle/supplementary transversal angle is 180° - 55° = 125°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Check arithmetic steps.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. 180° - 55° = 125°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. Consecutive interior angle gives 180° - 55° = 125°.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: Line segment BE acts as a transversal across parallel lines AB and EF[cite: 4]. The consecutive interior angle on the same side is 180° - 55° = 125°[cite: 4].

questions.question: Two parallel lines l and m are intersected by transversal t. Bisectors are drawn for two interior angles on the same side of the transversal. What angle do these two angle bisectors make with each other?[cite: 4]
questions.hint: Let the consecutive interior angles be 2x and 2y, where 2x + 2y = 180°.[cite: 4]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Half of 90° is 45°, but the triangle angle is 180° - 90° = 90°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. The bisectors form a right angle.[cite: 4]

Correct. Let the interior angles be 2x and 2y. Since lines are parallel, 2x + 2y = 180° ⇒ x + y = 90°. In the triangle formed by the transversal and the bisectors, the third angle is 180° - (x + y) = 180° - 90° = 90°.[cite: 4]
Incorrect. The bisectors intersect, so they cannot form a straight line.[cite: 4]

questions.explanation: The sum of interior angles on the same side is 180°[cite: 4]. The sum of their halves (the angles in the triangle formed by the bisectors) is \frac{180°}{2} = 90°[cite: 4]. Therefore, the third angle between the two bisectors is 180° - 90° = 90°[cite: 4].

questions.question: What is the parity of the sum of any two consecutive natural numbers?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: In any two consecutive numbers, one is even and one is odd.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Even + Odd is always odd.[cite: 3]
Correct. Between two consecutive natural numbers, one is always even and one is always odd; their sum is always odd.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. The alternation of even and odd guarantees an odd sum.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Natural numbers are strictly positive.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: Any two consecutive integers can be written as n and n + 1[cite: 3]. Their sum is 2n + 1, which is always an odd number[cite: 3].

questions.question: What is the general algebraic expression that generates the n^th odd natural number?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Multiply position n by 2 and subtract 1.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 2n generates even numbers.[cite: 3]
Correct. For n = 1, 2, 3\dots, 2n - 1 gives 1, 3, 5\dots, representing every odd number.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. For n = 2, this gives 4, which is even.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. For n = 3, this gives 8, which is even.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: Since the n^th even number is 2n, the n^th odd number is one less than the corresponding even number, yielding 2n - 1[cite: 3].

questions.question: What is the magic sum of a standard 3 × 3 magic square filled with the digits 1 through 9 without repetition?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Divide the total sum of numbers from 1 to 9 by the number of rows (3).[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 12 × 3 = 36 ≠ 45.[cite: 3]
Correct. The total sum of numbers 1 to 9 is 45. Dividing equally across 3 rows gives a magic sum of 45 ÷ 3 = 15.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 18 × 3 = 54 ≠ 45.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 34 is the magic sum of the 4 × 4 Chautīsa Yantra.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: The sum of all numbers from 1 to 9 is 9 × 10/2 = 45[cite: 3]. In a 3 × 3 magic square, all 3 rows have equal sums, so each row sums to 45/3 = 15[cite: 3].

questions.question: Which digit MUST occupy the central cell of any 3 × 3 magic square filled with numbers 1 to 9?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: The central number belongs to 4 lines (1 row, 1 column, 2 diagonals).[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 1 cannot form enough triples adding to 15.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Only the median value can balance 4 distinct lines.[cite: 3]
Correct. The center cell must be 5 because the magic sum is 3 × center, meaning 3 × 5 = 15.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 9 is too large to sit at the center.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: Adding the 4 lines passing through the center gives 4 × 15 = 60. The 9 cells sum to 45, with the center counted 3 extra times: 45 + 3c = 60 ⇒ 3c = 15 ⇒ c = 5[cite: 3].

questions.question: A light bulb is initially ON. If Dorjee toggles the switch exactly 77 times, what will the final state of the bulb be?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Consider the effect of an odd number of toggles on an initial ON state.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. An even number of toggles returns to ON, an odd number switches to OFF.[cite: 3]
Correct. 77 is an odd number. An odd number of state changes from ON results in OFF.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. This is a binary switch operation.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Parity determines the exact state.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: Each pair of 2 toggles leaves the bulb in its original state (ON)[cite: 3]. Since 77 = 2 × 38 + 1, there is 1 net toggle remaining, turning the bulb OFF[cite: 3].

questions.question: What is the parity of the sum of the first 100 positive integers (1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 100)?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Count how many odd numbers exist between 1 and 100.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. The sum is 5050, which is even.[cite: 3]
Correct. The series contains 50 odd numbers. The sum of an even number of odd numbers is always even.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 5050 is a composite number.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. The sum is strictly positive.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: There are 50 odd integers and 50 even integers in the first 100 numbers[cite: 3]. The sum of fifty odd numbers is even, and adding fifty even numbers maintains an even sum[cite: 3] (S = 100 × 101/2 = 5050, an even number)[cite: 3].

questions.question: Based on Case Study 2, what is the 9^th term of the Virahāṅka sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, \dots?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Add the 7th and 8th terms (21 + 34).[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. The terms are formed by addition of previous two terms, not adding 11.[cite: 3]
Correct. The 9^th term is 21 + 34 = 55.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 21 + 34 = 55.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 89 is the 10^th term (34 + 55).[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: Each term is the sum of the two preceding terms[cite: 3]. The 8^th term is 34 and the 7^th term is 21, so the 9^th term is 21 + 34 = 55[cite: 3].

questions.question: Based on Case Study 2, which repeating parity pattern governs the Virahāṅka sequence?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Write the parity of the first few terms: 1 (O), 2 (E), 3 (O), 5 (O), 8 (E)...[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Two odd numbers in a row occur (3, 5).[cite: 3]

options.text: Odd, Odd, Even, Odd, Odd, Even...
options.explanation: Incorrect. Check the starting terms: 1 is odd, 2 is even.[cite: 3]

options.text: Odd, Even, Odd, Odd, Even, Odd...
options.explanation: Correct. The parities repeat in cycles of 3: (Odd, Even, Odd), (Odd, Even, Odd)... because O + E = O, E + O = O, and O + O = E.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Even terms like 2, 8, 34 clearly exist.[cite: 3]

questions.correctAnswer: Odd, Even, Odd, Odd, Even, Odd...
questions.explanation: The terms have parities: 1 (O), 2 (E), 3 (O), 5 (O), 8 (E), 13 (O), 21 (O), 34 (E)... showing the recurring 3-block pattern: Odd, Even, Odd[cite: 3].
questions.answer: Odd, Even, Odd, Odd, Even, Odd...

questions.question: What is the famous 4 × 4 magic square inscribed at the Parshvanath Jain temple in Khajuraho called?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: The name is derived from its magic sum, 34.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Lo Shu is the ancient Chinese 3 × 3 grid.[cite: 3]
Correct. It is known as the Chautīsa Yantra because 'Chautīs' means 34, which is the magic sum of every row, column, and diagonal.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Kubera Yantra is a 3 × 3 yantra with magic sum 72.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Navagraha Yantras represent the nine planetary deities.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: The 10th-century 4 × 4 magic square at Khajuraho is named Chautīsa Yantra because each row, column, and diagonal adds up to 34 ('chautīs')[cite: 3].

questions.question: In the cryptarithm T + T + T = UT, where T and U are distinct single digits (0-9), what digit does T represent?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: We have 3 × T resulting in a two-digit number ending in T.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. If T = 0, UT is not a two-digit number.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 3 × 3 = 9, which is single-digit.[cite: 3]
Correct. 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, where U = 1 and T = 5.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 6 + 6 + 6 = 18, units digit is 8 ≠ 6.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: 3 × T must yield a units digit of T[cite: 3]. Testing single digits: 3 × 5 = 15, giving U = 1 and T = 5[cite: 3].

questions.question: What is the parity of the product of two odd numbers, such as 27 × 13?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Odd × Odd = ?[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. An even product requires at least one even factor.[cite: 3]
Correct. The product of two odd integers is always odd.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Neither factor is zero.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Multiplication parity is strictly deterministic.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: Since neither number contains a factor of 2, their product does not contain a factor of 2 and is therefore always odd[cite: 3].

questions.question: A staircase has 8 steps. A student can climb either 1 step or 2 steps at a time. In how many different ways can the student reach the top?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: The number of ways to climb n steps corresponds to the n^th Virahāṅka-Fibonacci number.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 21 is the number of ways for 7 steps.[cite: 3]
Correct. For n steps, the number of ways is given by Vₙ: V₁=1, V₂=2, V₃=3, V₄=5, V₅=8, V₆=13, V₇=21, V₈=34.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 55 is the number of ways for 9 steps.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. Check the additive recurrence rule.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: To reach step 8, one must take a single step from step 7 (21 ways) or a double step from step 6 (13 ways)[cite: 3]. Total ways = 21 + 13 = 34[cite: 3].

questions.question: If a 3 × 3 magic square has a center number m = 25, what is the magic sum of each row, column, and diagonal?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: In an algebraically generalized 3 × 3 magic square, the magic sum is 3m.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 50 = 2m.[cite: 3]
Correct. The magic sum is always 3 × m = 3 × 25 = 75.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 100 = 4m.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 125 = 5m.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: In any 3 × 3 magic square formed by consecutive terms centered at m, the magic sum is identically equal to 3m[cite: 3]. For m = 25, the magic sum is 3 × 25 = 75[cite: 3].

questions.question: In the cryptarithm UT + TA = TAT, where U, T, A are distinct digits, what are the values of U, T, and A?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Analyze the hundreds place of the 3-digit sum.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Correct. 91 + 10 = 101, which fits UT + TA = TAT perfectly with U=9, T=1, A=0.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 81 + 12 = 93, not a 3-digit number.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 92 + 21 = 113 ≠ 212.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 73 + 30 = 103 ≠ 303.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: The sum of two 2-digit numbers cannot exceed 99 + 99 = 198, so the hundreds digit T must be 1[cite: 3]. With T=1, U1 + 1A = 1A1[cite: 3]. Units column: 1 + A ends in 1 ⇒ A = 0[cite: 3]. Tens column: U + 1 = 10 ⇒ U = 9[cite: 3]. Checking: 91 + 10 = 101[cite: 3].

questions.question: Two consecutive terms in the Virahāṅka sequence are 987 and 1597. What is the term immediately preceding 987, and what is the term immediately following 1597?[cite: 3]
questions.hint: Use Vₙ₋₁ = Vₙ₊₁ - Vₙ to go backward and Vₙ₊₂ = Vₙ + Vₙ₊₁ to go forward.[cite: 3]

options.explanation: Correct. Preceding: 1597 - 987 = 610. Following: 987 + 1597 = 2584.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 377 is two steps before 987.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 987 + 1597 = 2584, not 3194.[cite: 3]
Incorrect. 1597 - 987 = 610.[cite: 3]

questions.explanation: By the recurrence relation: the preceding term is 1597 - 987 = 610, and the following term is 987 + 1597 = 2584[cite: 3].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: According to the Triangle Inequality property, which condition must hold true for any three side lengths a, b, and c to form a valid triangle?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: The straight direct path must always be shorter than the roundabout path.[cite: 2]

options.text: The sum of any two sides must be less than the third side
options.explanation: Incorrect. If the sum is less, the arcs do not meet.[cite: 2]

options.text: The sum of any two sides must be strictly greater than the third side
options.explanation: Correct. For a triangle to exist, the sum of any two side lengths must be strictly greater than the third side (a + b > c).[cite: 2]

options.text: The sum of any two sides must equal the third side
options.explanation: Incorrect. If equal, the points are collinear (circles touch at a single point on the line).[cite: 2]

options.text: The square of two sides equals the third side
options.explanation: Incorrect. That relates to the Pythagorean theorem for right triangles, not general existence.[cite: 2]

questions.correctAnswer: The sum of any two sides must be strictly greater than the third side
questions.explanation: A triangle can only exist if the direct path between any two vertices is shorter than the roundabout path through the third vertex, meaning a + b > c for all sides[cite: 2].
questions.answer: The sum of any two sides must be strictly greater than the third side

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: Which of the following sets of side lengths CANNOT form a triangle?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: Check if the sum of the two smallest sides is greater than the longest side.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 3 + 4 = 7 > 5, forms a triangle.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. 5 + 5 = 10 > 8, forms an isosceles triangle.[cite: 2]
Correct. 2 + 3 = 5 < 6. The sum of the two shorter sides is less than the third side, making a triangle impossible.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. 10 + 20 = 30 > 25, forms a triangle.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: Since 2 + 3 = 5 which is strictly less than the longest side 6, circles drawn from the endpoints with radii 2 cm and 3 cm will never intersect[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: What is the sum of the three interior angles of any triangle on a plane?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: Recall Euclid's proof using a line drawn parallel to the base through the opposite vertex.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 90° is a right angle.[cite: 2]
Correct. The interior angles of any triangle always add up to 180°.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. Three angles forming a triangle sum to 180°.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. 360° is the angle sum of a quadrilateral.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: Drawing a parallel line through one vertex creates alternate interior angles equal to the base angles; together with the vertex angle, they form a straight line (180°)[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: In \triangle ABC, the exterior angle at vertex C is ∠ ACD = 110°. If one of the interior opposite angles is ∠ B = 60°, what is the measure of ∠ A?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: An exterior angle equals the sum of its two interior opposite angles.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. That would make the exterior angle 120°.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. 70° is the adjacent interior angle ∠ ACB.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. Check the exterior angle relationship.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles: ∠ A + 60° = 110° ⇒ ∠ A = 50°[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: What is an altitude of a triangle?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: Consider the line segment showing the true perpendicular height from a vertex.[cite: 2]

options.text: A line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is the median of the triangle.[cite: 2]

options.text: A perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension)
options.explanation: Correct. An altitude is the perpendicular dropped from a vertex to the opposite line/side.[cite: 2]

options.text: A ray that divides an angle into two equal parts
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is an angle bisector.[cite: 2]

options.text: The line segment connecting midpoints of two sides
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is a mid-segment.[cite: 2]

questions.correctAnswer: A perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension)
questions.explanation: An altitude is defined as the perpendicular line segment dropped from a vertex of the triangle to the opposite side (or line containing the opposite side)[cite: 2].
questions.answer: A perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension)

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: In which type of triangle do two of the altitudes coincide exactly with two of its sides?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: Think about where two sides already meet at a 90° angle.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Altitudes in equilateral triangles lie in the interior.[cite: 2]
Correct. In a right-angled triangle, the two perpendicular legs serve directly as the altitudes for each other.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. Altitudes in obtuse triangles fall outside the triangle.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. All three altitudes lie entirely inside an acute-angled triangle.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: In a right-angled triangle, the two sides containing the right angle are perpendicular to each other, so each serves as the altitude to the other[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: Can a triangle have more than one obtuse angle?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: An obtuse angle is strictly greater than 90°.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Two obtuse angles exceed 180°.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. The type of sides does not change the angle sum of 180°.[cite: 2]
Correct. If a triangle had two obtuse angles, their sum would exceed 90° + 90° = 180°, violating the angle sum property.[cite: 2]

options.text: Only if side lengths are large
options.explanation: Incorrect. Angles are independent of scale.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: Since each obtuse angle is > 90°, two obtuse angles would sum to > 180°, leaving no positive degree measure for the third angle[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: Two known sides of a triangle measure 3 cm and 7 cm. Which of the following CANNOT be the length of the third side?[cite: 2]
questions.hint: The third side x must satisfy |7 - 3| < x < 7 + 3.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 4 < 5 < 10, which is valid.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. 4 < 8 < 10, which is valid.[cite: 2]
Correct. If the side is 4 cm, 3 + 4 = 7, which is not strictly greater than 7.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. 4 < 6.4 < 10, which is valid.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: The third side must strictly lie between 7 - 3 = 4 cm and 7 + 3 = 10 cm[cite: 2]. A length of 4 cm gives 3 + 4 = 7, collapsing into a straight line segment rather than a triangle[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: Why is it impossible to construct a triangle with angles 70°, 70°, and 70°?[cite: 2]

options.text: Because triangles cannot have acute angles

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: When constructing a triangle given two side lengths and the included angle, under what condition is the construction impossible?[cite: 2]

options.text: If the included angle is acute
options.explanation: Incorrect. Acute included angles always form valid triangles.[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. That simply constructs an isosceles triangle.[cite: 2]

options.text: If one side is longer than the other

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: Where does the altitude drawn from vertex T to the line containing base RY lie in triangle TRY with ∠ R = 140°?[cite: 2]

options.explanation: Incorrect. Altitudes to sides adjacent to an obtuse angle fall outside the triangle.[cite: 2]

options.text: Outside the triangle, on the extension of side YR

Incorrect. That only happens if ∠ R = 90°.[cite: 2]

questions.answer: Outside the triangle, on the extension of side YR

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
questions.question: In a right-angled triangle ABC with ∠ B = 90°, the hypotenuse AC = 5 cm. How many non-congruent right-angled triangles can be constructed with this hypotenuse?[cite: 2]

Incorrect. There are infinitely many points on Thales' semicircle.[cite: 2]
Correct. Angle ∠ A can take any value strictly between 0° and 90°, yielding infinitely many non-congruent triangles.[cite: 2]
Incorrect. Real right triangles with hypotenuse 5 exist.[cite: 2]

questions.explanation: Any point on the semicircle with diameter AC forms a right angle at B[cite: 2]. Since there are infinitely many points on the semicircle, infinitely many distinct right triangles exist[cite: 2].

questions.category: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

Incorrect. Three 90° angles sum to 270°.[cite: 2]

questions.correctAnswer: No, because every equilateral triangle must have all three angles equal to 60°, which is strictly acute

questions.answer: No, because every equilateral triangle must have all three angles equal to 60°, which is strictly acute

questions.question: Based on Case Study 3, how many times will the second fountain fill the cistern in one full day?[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Divide 1 day by 1/2 day.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Incorrect. If it fills in half a day, it fills more than once in a full day.[cite: 1]
Correct. 1 ÷ 1/2 = 1 × 2 = 2 times.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. 4 times is the rate for the third fountain.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: The second fountain fills the cistern in 1/2 day, so in 1 full day it fills the cistern 1 ÷ 1/2 = 2 times[cite: 1].

questions.question: Based on Case Study 3, how many times will all four fountains running together fill the cistern in a single day?[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Add the individual rates: 1 + 2 + 4 + 5.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Incorrect. 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12.[cite: 1]
Correct. First fountain: 1 time; Second: 2 times; Third: 4 times; Fourth: 5 times. Sum = 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12 times.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Check arithmetic sum.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. The total rate is 12 cisterns per day.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: In one day, the four fountains fill the cistern 1 + (1 ÷ 1/2) + (1 ÷ 1/4) + (1 ÷ 1/5) = 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12 times[cite: 1].

questions.question: Based on Case Study 3, how long will it take for the four fountains flowing together to fill the cistern once?[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Take the reciprocal of the combined daily filling rate.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Correct. Since they fill 12 cisterns in 1 day, 1 cistern takes 1 ÷ 12 = 1/12 of a day (2 hours).[cite: 1]
Incorrect. The combined rate is 12, not 10.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Flowing together they are faster, not slower.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. 1 ÷ 12 = 1/12.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: Since the four fountains together fill 12 cisterns per day, the time required to fill one cistern is 1/12 of a day[cite: 1].

questions.question: Simplify the product to its lowest terms: 14/15 × 25/42.[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Cancel common factors between numerators and denominators before multiplying.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Correct. Divide 14 and 42 by 14 (giving 1 and 3), and divide 25 and 15 by 5 (giving 5 and 3). Then 1 × 5/3 × 3 = 5/9.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Canceling factors leaves 5 in numerator and 9 in denominator.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Check prime factor cancellations.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. This is not simplified to lowest terms.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: Dividing 14 and 42 by 14 gives 1 and 3[cite: 1]. Dividing 25 and 15 by 5 gives 5 and 3[cite: 1]. The product becomes 1 × 5/3 × 3 = 5/9[cite: 1].

questions.question: Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 93/5 ft and breadth is 33/4 ft.[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Convert mixed fractions to improper fractions: 48/5 × 15/4.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Incorrect. That is only 9 × 3.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Check cross-cancellation.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. The exact product is 36.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: Area = length × breadth = 48/5 × 15/4 = 48 × 15/5 × 4 = 12 × 3 = 36 sq. ft.[cite: 1]

questions.question: The government acquired 1/6 of Somu's ancestral farmland to construct a highway. Of the remaining land, she gave 1/2 to her daughter Krishna and 1/3 to her son Bora, retaining the rest. What fraction of the original land remains with Somu?[cite: 1]
questions.hint: First calculate remaining land 5/6, then find the fraction Somu kept: 1 - (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6 of the remainder.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Correct. Remaining after road = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6. Somu retains 1 - (1/2 + 1/3) = 1 - 5/6 = 1/6 of this remainder. Total kept = 1/6 × 5/6 = 5/36.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. 5/18 is the share given to Bora.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. 5/12 is the share given to Krishna.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Check arithmetic steps.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: Remaining land after highway acquisition is 1 - 1/6 = 5/6[cite: 1]. Children's combined share of remainder is 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6[cite: 1]. Somu keeps the remaining 1 - 5/6 = 1/6 of the 5/6, which equals 1/6 × 5/6 = 5/36 of the original land[cite: 1].

questions.question: Evaluate the telescoping product: (1 - 1/2) × (1 - 1/3) × (1 - 1/4) × \dots × (1 - 1/10).[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Rewrite each factor as n-1/n and observe numerator-denominator cancellations.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Incorrect. That is only the first factor.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Check cancellations carefully.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. All numerators cancel with preceding denominators except the first numerator 1 and last denominator 10.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: Writing the factors out: 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 4/5 \dots × 9/10[cite: 1]. Every intermediate numerator cancels with the previous denominator, leaving solely 1/10[cite: 1].

questions.question: In Bhāskarāchārya's *Līlāvatī* (1150 CE), a problem states: A miser gave a beggar 1/5  of  1/16  of  1/4  of  1/2  of  2/3  of  3/4 of a silver dramma. If 1 dramma = 1280 cowrie shells, how many cowrie shells did the beggar receive?[cite: 1]
questions.hint: Multiply all fractions together, cancel common factors, and multiply by 1280.[cite: 1]

options.explanation: Correct. Product = 1 × 2 × 3 × 1 × 1 × 1/2 × 3 × 4 × 5 × 16 × 4 = 6/7680 = 1/1280 of a dramma. Since 1 dramma = 1280 shells, 1/1280 × 1280 = 1 shell.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. 1/1280 × 1280 = 1.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. Check denominator simplification.[cite: 1]
Incorrect. The humor in Bhāskara's problem is that the miser gave exactly the smallest single coin.[cite: 1]

questions.explanation: Evaluating the product of fractions: 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 1/5 × 1/16 × 1/4 = 1/4 × 1/5 × 1/16 × 1/4 = 1/1280 of a dramma[cite: 1]. Multiplying by the conversion factor of 1280 shells/dramma yields exactly 1 cowrie shell[cite: 1].
